what: Sound Meter turns your device microphone into a simple decibel meter. It shows the current sound level in large numbers, the minimum, average and maximum since you started, and a graph of the last 60 seconds.

It measures the digital level from your microphone exactly (in dBFS) and adds a calibration offset to estimate the sound level in decibels. Microphones differ, so the estimate is approximate unless you calibrate it once against a real meter.
You can choose A-weighting (dB(A), like the human ear) or flat (dB(Z)), fast or slow response, and download your readings as a CSV file. Nothing is recorded or uploaded.
uses: Check how loud traffic, neighbours or appliances are.
Compare rooms to find the quietest place to work.
See if a concert, workshop or headphones are getting too loud.
Check background noise before you record a podcast or video.
Measure how sound gets quieter with distance.
Compare the noise of fans, vacuum cleaners or hair dryers.
tutorial: Press "Start microphone" and allow access when your browser asks. The big number starts to move.
Point the microphone (usually at the bottom of a phone) towards the sound and keep the device still. Do not cover the microphone.
The big number is the current level. Minimum, Average (Leq) and Maximum cover the time since you pressed Start or Reset.
A-weighting matches how people hear noise; flat counts all frequencies equally. Fast follows quick changes, Slow gives a steadier reading.
If you have a real sound level meter, type its reading into "I know the real level now is" and press Calibrate. The offset is saved for this device.
Press "Download readings (CSV)" to save one reading per second with the time, to open in a spreadsheet.
features: Average is the true energy average (Leq), as on real meters.
See how the noise changes over time.
dB(A) filter built to the standard curve.
Match a real meter once; the offset is remembered.
See the exact digital level for audio work.
One reading per second for spreadsheets.

example.title: Worked example: checking a noisy bedroom
example.text: Mia thinks traffic keeps her awake. She puts her phone on the windowsill at 11 pm, presses Start microphone and chooses Slow response and dB(A). After ten minutes the meter shows a minimum of 34, an average of 43 and a maximum of 68 dB(A) when a lorry passed. She downloads the CSV to show the peaks to her landlord, noting that a phone gives an estimate, not a certified measurement.

tips: Turn off "voice isolation" or noise reduction features on your device if you can; they change the level.
Calibrate once with a real meter in a steady noise for the best accuracy.
Use Slow response for steady noise and Fast for short sounds such as claps.
Do not use it to prove a legal noise limit; use a certified Class 1 or Class 2 meter for that.
Phone microphones often cannot measure very loud sounds above about 100 dB accurately.
problems: The microphone may be muted, blocked or used by another app. Check that the browser has microphone access and try another microphone from the list.
The readings seem too high or too low
Every microphone is different. Calibrate against a real meter, or treat the value as a rough guide.
It says microphone access was blocked
Click the lock or microphone icon next to the web address, allow the microphone, then press Start again.
Loud sounds all read about the same
The microphone has reached its maximum (near 0 dBFS). Move further away from the sound.
